narrative:
The model estimated a 43% chance that you would become a bad credit risk. Although that is below an even chance, it is still a substantial risk level and exceeded the lender’s threshold for approval, so the application was denied.

The strongest factor was the 48-month repayment period you requested, far longer than the average approved applicant’s roughly 19 months. A longer commitment gives more time for financial circumstances to change, so it pushed the decision toward bad credit risk. Your credit record was the second most important factor. It showed critical or other credits rather than a clean record of existing paid credit; about one-third of approved applicants have a similar rating, though more have existing paid credit. In this case, this factor actually leaned toward good credit and reduced the risk estimate. The third factor was your checking account balance of 0–200 DM. This is less common than having no account and suggests a limited cash buffer, so it added to the risk assessment.

To strengthen a future application, consider requesting a smaller amount or a shorter repayment term, building a steadier checking or savings balance, and reviewing your credit history for errors or unpaid items. You could also ask the lender what specific policy threshold you missed and whether adding a guarantor or co-applicant would help.
